utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we go into closed session to continue the examination-in-chief of Witness D9, I would like to inform the Prosecution that the request to be allowed to respond to the Davidovic submissions is currently considered by the Chamber and we hope to inform you as soon as possible whether or not we'll allow you to respond. If there's no other procedural issue at this moment raised, then we'll turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just before we do that, could I just ask how that request was relayed to the Chamber, because I personally wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I understood, that it was an informal request. It might be -- the situation might not be entirely clear. When we're talking about motions, it's clear that the other party can respond and that for further submissions you'd need the approval of the Chamber, whereas here, of course, the Chamber invited the Defence to make submissions, and from what I understood it was, from a procedural point of view, not entirely clear to the Prosecution whether this was the situation in which they were entitled to respond. That's what -- and I did understand that it was an informal request addressed to the legal officers and then, of course, the Chamber would have to decide. But if there's anything you'd like to raise in this respect, then, Mr. Josse --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think I would, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think I would, Your Honour. I know generally Mr. Stewart deals with these sort of things, but if a request like that is going to be made informally and then there is going to be, and I mean this in a very neutral sense, a public pronouncement about it, surely the Defence need to know before that public pronouncement is made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the words I used were not the proper ones because perhaps I should have said that where the Prosecution sought clarification of its procedural position in respect of Davidovic, specifically in view of the question whether this was a matter where they were entitled to respond, that that's considered by the Chamber. I do not and the Chamber does not consider this matter to be like a request for further submissions in addition to what the Rules allow. But if there's anything, of course it's -- please, if Mr. Stewart would like to say something about it, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've made my observation and I'll certainly discuss it with him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will wait to hear from the Trial Chamber because we are currently in the drafting stage, but we will not file anything until we hear from the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the reason why --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's also not make the procedural issue -- I mean, the Davidovic issue as such is important enough not to be buried under additional procedural issues. The Chamber very much would like to focus on the substance rather than on the, I would say, satellite problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And as the Court is well aware, the Defence regard this as a very serious issue as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, let's try to focus as much as possible on the substance and ... We could then now turn into closed session, or were we already?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We now turn into closed session. That's how it ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The issue I would like to briefly raise is the response to the submissions in relation to the -- what I would call the Davidovic matter. The Defence has asked not to take any decision before the Defence has had a opportunity on whether or not the Prosecution would be allowed to respond. To be quite honest, the Chamber is very much inclined to give an opportunity to the Defence -- to the Prosecution to respond, but since we promised that you would make any submissions, the Chamber nevertheless will say a few words about it. From the submissions the Chamber has received, it appears -- or at least we could not exclude that the issue is wrongly understood. Why can't we say you understand the issue wrongly or not? Because the Chamber has been confronted with requests for further delay to provide further material. So since we do not know what that material will be, we cannot make a final assessment at this moment whether you understand the issue right or wrong. Let me clarify what the issue is. The issue is the following: Mr. Davidovic was cross-examined in a way which included, well, to say at the least, strong words. The issue is whether the Defence had a sufficient factual basis of this rather firm treatment of Mr. Davidovic. The Chamber wanted to find out what material the Defence exactly had at that moment which would justify such strong words. The Chamber asked for it and was confronted with, at least to some extent, an answer which says this is privileged, this is privileged material, so we can't tell you. The Chamber wondered whether the material the Defence would rely upon would be really privileged. If, for example, this would be public broadcasting, then the Chamber still had difficulties to understand how that material could in any way be privileged. Therefore, the Chamber asked the Defence to further explain its position in this context. The fear is that the Defence might understand the issue to be how to undermine the testimony of Mr. Davidovic. If the Defence had no sufficient material to approach Mr. Davidovic as it did, that of course does not automatically mean that if you have no material to say that he's a thief or a criminal or a liar, that doesn't mean that therefore he never has stolen in his life, he has never lied in his life. We do not know. What we should avoid is that the challenging of the testimony of Mr. Davidovic will be mixed up with the procedural issue we are discussing, the procedural issue being limited to whether at that time the material was such that it justified the way in which Mr. Davidovic was questioned. It may well turn out, at least that's a possibility, that if the Defence had no reason at that moment to put so bluntly to Mr. Davidovic that he was a liar or a criminal or a thief or -- that in the presentation of the Defence case, that at a later stage you'd come up with some evidence establishing that perhaps he was or he was not, but even if at a later stage the Defence would be able to establish that part or the whole of the testimony of Mr. Davidovic is unreliable and incredible, that as such does not justify the way questions were put to Mr. Davidovic. So therefore, we are at this moment - and that's the issue raised by the Prosecution - we are focusing on the procedural issue on whether at that moment the Defence had satisfactory reasons which would justify the way in which Mr. Davidovic was examined. That's the issue and nothing else at this moment. Of course the Chamber will receive whatever evidence there is to establish that Mr. Davidovic would not have been a reliable witness or not be a credible witness. Therefore, the Chamber is a bit surprised that the Defence wants to first consider this matter. If after a couple of -- not to consider the matter but to make further submissions. If at the time material was available, whether or not privileged, the Chamber does not see how we have to wait for another considerable period of time to find out what that material was, because as the matter as defined relates to what the Defence at that time had available as material justifying the way in which it questioned Mr. Davidovic. So therefore, the Chamber is anxious not to confuse the matters. Until now in the submissions, the perspectives are that we will receive at a later stage other material, which is surprising because if it was there at the time -- not whether you gained it at a later stage, and whether you want to use that material in contesting the truthfulness of Mr. Davidovic's testimony, that's a totally different matter; you can introduce that material during the presentation of the Defence case. But the Chamber really wonders why a brief response at this moment by the Prosecution, why it takes such an effort to make up your mind whether that could be granted or not, especially in view of the response of the Defence which is a question, as a matter of fact, tells us that we'll -- that you have to do a lot of work on that material first, and we haven't heard anything about the privilege any more. So therefore, we are a bit confused. I suggest that the Defence makes up its mind by, let's say, tomorrow whether there's any need to -- or whether it would object against a response to be given by the Prosecution; and if you would object, the Chamber would like to hear in five minutes, not more, what that objection is based on in view of the issue as I defined it a couple of minutes ago. Then after that, the Chamber will decide whether or not it will follow its inclination to grant the Prosecution an opportunity to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I say four things. First of all, yes, it's true that Mr. Stewart is heavily involved in this and perhaps I need to speak to him; but secondly, wires have got crossed here. Although Mr. Stewart has not been involved in any activity this morning, speaking for myself, I don't possibly object to the Prosecution replying. I don't know how I could possibly object. The more submissions, the more information this Court has, the better. So without conferring with him, I make the decision on behalf of the Defence that the Chamber should welcome further submissions from the parties in relation to this matter. Secondly, what the Defence are asking for is ultimately an oral hearing before any action or decision is taken by the Chamber. Partly what Your Honour has just said to us is illustrative of why that is important, so that the issues can be refined and defined and the Defence can address any submissions to the issues that are of concern to the Chamber. And my third observation, which is straying slightly, is of course we'll consider what Your Honour says, but what the Defence, again speaking for myself, is not clear about is where this is all going, what's the purpose of this at this stage of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mainly to establish whether or not it was fair to treat Mr. Davidovic as he was treated by the Defence. Whether there were fair reasons. If a witness comes in here and if the first question is, "Are you a criminal?" then the Chamber will not allow to put that question to the witness. If during the examination-in-chief it develops in a certain way, there might be a moment to say, "Well, I have in front of me five convictions. Isn't it true that you're just an ordinary criminal instead of the religious leader as you claim?" That's of course -- it very much depends on the circumstances, but main issue raised by the Prosecution is, "We don't want our witnesses to be treated in this way, which may have all kinds of effects if there is no good reason to do so." I think that's the main issue. So the first and utmost purpose of this whole exercise is to establish whether Mr. Davidovic was treated in a way in which he should not have been treated or whether it was justified to treat him in the way as the Defence treated him. That's issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd simply say that I'd urge the Chamber to consider setting an hour aside the week after next for oral submissions in relation to this. That's what I would content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, this Chamber has now waited for month and month and month on settlement of the Davidovic matter and the Chamber is not willing to drag this along for a longer period of time, especially, I mean, also in view of the written submissions made at this moment. This is not a decision not to say that we will not grant an opportunity, but as I said in the beginning, it is a procedural matter which is not without importance, but it's that procedural matter and it's not the testimony of Mr. Davidovic in general and whether it's true or not, whether it should be given a lot of -- whether it should be believed to be true or not, that's a totally different matter. It's the way in which witnesses are treated in this courtroom. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least if -- we can take one further step and that is that the Prosecution may respond to the submissions made by the Defence, and the Chamber will further consider the request for further oral argument, and if there's anything in that respect the Prosecution would like to raise, they can do that right away in their response.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour has summarised very succinctly and very clearly our concerns in respect of the filing that we received yesterday. We believe the matter's been pending before this Court for many, many months. The issue has been clear. It has been articulated time and time again. It's our position, Your Honour, that there is no additional -- there is no need for additional submissions on this matter. Our position is it needs to be resolved, it needs to be resolved quickly, and we submit, Your Honour, that there has been either an unwillingness to answer -- address the issue or there's been a lack of clarity, but there's been sufficient time. And we would request that the Court make a decision on this matter based on the evidence before it and the matters that have been -- that have come before it in the pleadings that have come before it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I have to understand this is, because then I wouldn't say it's a comedy of errors, but that the Prosecution withdraws its request to respond? If so, because it's only two minutes ago that Mr. Josse gave up his opposition and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're prepared to make our submission if the Court grants us that request, but in many ways Your Honour has summarised what we'll be saying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you write down in that decision approximately what I said, that is what is the issue, what information did we receive, and is the matter of the privilege addressed, yes or no? If it would be limited to that and if it would be concurrent with what I just said, then of course I'll think over during the next weekend what happens if the Chamber identifies an issue almost identical to the Prosecution whether that is an alarming sign or not -- well it could be, it could not be, but then there's no need to sit down and write down what has been said and what, as I do understand now, is agreed upon by the -- by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I haven't seen our final written submission, Your Honour, because I've been in Court, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you -- I'm not urging the Prosecution to do it. If you look at what is prepared now and you think it would add anything, you have an opportunity to do so within the next -- well, we're not sitting next week anyhow, but let's say by next Tuesday. And I'd very much like the Defence to carefully consider what they'd like to raise during oral argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know it's late, but perhaps again it would help. What I'm not clear about is what the consequences are of the Chamber agreeing with the Prosecution's submissions. That really is essential for an advocate to understand how it's going to affect his client, and that's what I'm afraid I personally don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It doesn't go any further than we say this is not what should have been done to Mr. Davidovic, which of course implies that the next time the Defence would carefully consider whether there are good reasons to use such strong language. But if you're asking me whether that would mean that the evidence could not be challenged any more or whether -- it's just a procedural matter of the way in which witnesses are treated in this courtroom. It doesn't say anything in terms of evaluation of the evidence, exclusion of -- what do you have in mind as alternative? Should we exclude that evidence? We would have difficulties to do that because it would create exactly the situation which we would like to avoid, that is that by the way of questioning a witness doesn't feel free any more to give the answers. So it's not entirely clear what other consequences you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think that -- that's why I, speaking again for myself, so anxious to have a brief oral hearing because I -- perhaps if I could use an English metaphor, to lance the boil, because I am somewhat uncertain, as I've already said, where all this is going. Your Honour, the fact of the matter is I -- we conceded in the submission that the most serious allegation in one sense had no foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But the -- what the submission tried to emphasise is even if there had been no material provided by investigators or anyone else, based on Mr. Krajisnik's instructions, we would have suggested that this witness was an out-and-out liar. So far as the criminal bit is concerned, well, frankly our information was that he was involved in some of the activities that he was alleging our client was involved in. That must mean that he's a criminal. It's as simple as that in one sense. So far as the detail is concerned, well, to a limited extent the submission deals with that. That's really how I would put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the question quite simply is that if Mr. Krajisnik tells you that someone is lying, would that justify to call him a liar in court if he testifies different from -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely, because I urge the Chamber to remember what the witness was saying that Mr. Krajisnik had done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik said that's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And certainly where I come from, in those circumstances you must call someone a liar. For an advocate to fail to do that would upset a Judge to no end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I now better understand what your point is. There seems to be quite a difference in practice between the different versions of the adversarial system. Well, fortunately, we're not bound to any of these, neither to even non-adversarial systems. The Chamber will further consider the matter, it's clear. And if the Prosecution would like to respond, then please do it within the next five days, I would say. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until tomorrow morning, with the apologies to interpreters and technicians. 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of November, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.00 p.m.,
